'''''Araucaria cunninghamii''''' is a species of [[conifer]] in the family [[Araucariaceae]], known as '''hoop pine'''. Other less commonly used names include '''colonial pine''', '''Queensland pine''',<ref>{{cite web |title=Hoop Pine |url=https://www.daf.qld.gov.au/forestry/using-wood-and-its-benefits/wood-properties-of-timber-trees/hoop-pine |publisher=Queensland Department of Agriculture and Fisheries |access-date=23 March 2017 |archive-date=25 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170225020455/https://www.daf.qld.gov.au/forestry/using-wood-and-its-benefits/wood-properties-of-timber-trees/hoop-pine }}</ref> '''Dorrigo pine''', '''Moreton Bay pine''' and '''Richmond River pine'''.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> The scientific name honours the [[botanist]] and [[explorer]] [[Allan Cunningham (botanist)|Allan Cunningham]], who collected the first specimens in the 1820s. It is the earliest-diverging extant lineage within the genus Araucaria, and the only species within section Eutacta native to continental mainland areas; all other species in the section are naturally confined to islands.<ref>[https://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/pleins_textes_7/b_fdi_53-54/010017121.pdf Phylogenetic relationships within Araucariaceae based on rbcL gene sequences]</ref>

==Description==
The [[leaf|leaves]] on young trees are awl-shaped, 1–2 cm long, about 2 mm thick at the base, and scale-like, incurved, 1–2 cm long and 4 mm broad on mature trees. The [[conifer cone|cones]] are ovoid, 8–10 cm long and 6–8 cm diameter, and take about 18 months to mature. They disintegrate at maturity to release the nut-like edible [[seed]]s.

==Subspecies==
There are two varieties:
*''Araucaria cunninghamii'' var. ''cunninghamii'' – Australia, from northeast [[New South Wales]] to east-central [[Queensland]], at 0–1,000 m elevation.
*''Araucaria cunninghamii'' var. ''papuana'' – New Guinea, on the mountains of [[Papua New Guinea]], and in [[Irian Jaya]], [[Indonesia]], at 100–2,700 m elevation.

==Habitat==
The species is found in the dry [[rainforest]]s of [[New South Wales]] and [[Queensland]] and in [[New Guinea]]. The trees can live up to 450 years and grow to a height of 60 metres.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hoop Pine |url=http://about.nsw.gov.au/encyclopedia/article/hoop-pine/ |publisher=about NSW |access-date=25 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110313145805/http://about.nsw.gov.au/encyclopedia/article/hoop-pine/ |archive-date=13 March 2011 }}</ref>  The bark is rough, splits naturally, and peels easily.<ref>{{cite web|title=Species: Araucaria cunninghamii (Hoop Pine)|url=http://adl.brs.gov.au/mapserv/plant/species.phtml?speciesid=3 |publisher=Plantation Information Network |access-date=25 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120318130323/http://adl.brs.gov.au/mapserv/plant/species.phtml?speciesid=3 |archive-date=18 March 2012 }}</ref>

Examples of the species can be found on ridges and mountaintops in Queensland's [[North Burnett Region|North Burnett]] region (sometimes in quantity where dry rainforests remain – such as on the summit of [[Mount Perry, Queensland|Mount Perry]] and on ridges north of [[Mount Walsh National Park]]), inland from [[Gympie]] in the Wide Bay, and also at lower elevations around homesteads, where the trees may possibly have been retained for aesthetic value. An example can be seen off the road to the lookout above the town of Mount Perry and a number of trees line the approach to the town from [[Gin Gin, Queensland|Gin Gin]].

==Cultivation and other uses==
The [[wood]] is a high-quality timber that is particularly important to the plywood industry and also used for [[furniture]], [[Wood veneer|veneer]], [[joiner]]y, [[panelling]], [[particle board]], [[flooring]] and [[boat]]s.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hoop Pine|url=http://www.timber.net.au/?option=com_species&name=Hoop%20Pine&Itemid=434|website=Australian Timber Database|publisher=Timber.net.au|access-date=25 August 2012}}</ref>  Most natural stands in Australia and Papua New Guinea have been depleted by logging. It is now mainly found on timber [[plantation]]s; however, the species continues to thrive in protected areas, including [[Lamington National Park]] where at least one walking track is named after it.<ref>{{cite web|title=Nature, culture and history |url=http://www.derm.qld.gov.au/parks/lamington/culture.html |publisher=Queensland Government |access-date=25 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120814190346/http://www.derm.qld.gov.au/parks/lamington/culture.html |archive-date=14 August 2012 }}</ref>

[[Indigenous Australians|Aboriginal Australians]] used the [[resin]] as cement.<ref>{{cite web|last=Corlett |first=Eloise |title=An Evolution Of Ethnobotany |url=http://www.byronbaynow.com/selah.html |publisher=ByronBayNow |access-date=25 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110218231740/http://www.byronbaynow.com/selah.html |archive-date=18 February 2011 }}</ref>

===Pests===
The plantations in Queensland have been subject to damage by a native rat species, ''[[Rattus tunneyi]]'', which digs to the roots of a semi-mature tree and kills it. The animal was declared a pest for this reason.<ref name="Baverstock1983">{{cite encyclopedia|last = Baverstock |first = P.R. |author-link = P. R. Baverstock |editor-last = Strahan |editor-first = R. |editor-link = Ronald Strahan |encyclopedia = Complete book of Australian mammals. [[National Photographic Index of Australian Wildlife|The national photographic index of Australian wildlife]] |title = Pale Field Rat ''Rattus Tunneyi'' |edition = 1 |year = 1983 |publisher = Angus & Robertson |location = London |isbn = 0-207-14454-0 |page = 451}}</ref> The vulnerability of ''A. cunninghamii'' plantations to pest losses has caused some of them to be replaced by ''[[Araucaria hunsteinii|A. hunsteinii]]'', which suffers less in plantation.<ref name="Wylie-1982" /> Unspecified [[Microlepidoptera]] are significant pests of the [[conifer cone|pinecone]]s of both.<ref group="Gressitt 1982" name="Microlepidoptera" />

====Biological control====
''[[Cryptolaemus montrouzieri]]'' is a [[coccinellidae|coccinellid]] predator of [[mealybug]] and soft [[scale insect]] parasites of ''A. cunninghamii'', and has several characteristics that make it a good [[biological control|biocontrol]] for use in plantations.<ref name="Finlay-Doney-Walter-2012" /> Although they are less interested in other trees – by many multiples – ''C. montrouzieri'' does hunt the same pests in [[custard apple]] and [[citrus]] plantations.<ref name="Finlay-Doney-Walter-2012" />
